note: Which Magadha ruler was known as 'Seniya' (official key: Bimbisara). Bimbisara is taught as a powerful Magadha ruler (fess105 p. 48; lehs102 p. 31), but the epithet 'Seniya' appears in neither NCERT source fetched, nor is it in the WBBSE books reachable from this machine. Source gap; the magadha_rise exam_note states the exam answer (Bimbisara) openly and flags that the books do not carry the title.

The famous physician during Buddha's time was Jivaka (official key). Primary chapter HIS-05 (Buddha's time); mapped here only as alt. Jivaka is named in neither fess105, fess106 nor lehs102. Source gap; not taught in this chapter.

Which kingdom covered the modern Patna and Gaya districts (official key: Magadha). Taught via Magadha's capitals Rajagriha/Rajgir and Pataliputra/present-day Patna in present-day Bihar (fess105 p. 48; lehs102 pp. 31). Partly: the Gaya district detail is not stated verbatim in the NCERT pages used; the Patna anchor and Bihar location are.

Clan-capital matching (Moriyas-Pippalivana, Videhas-Mithila, Licchavis-Vaishali, Mallas-Kapilavastu; official key: only d-4 is wrongly matched). Primary HIS-04 with alt HIS-05. Only partly supported by the sources: Licchavis are taught as part of the Vajji sangha whose capital was Vaishali (fess105 p. 48; fess106 p. 56), the Buddha is taught as a Sakya (fess106 p. 52) and NCERT Map 1 places Kusinagara with Malla (lehs102 p. 30) — enough to see Malla-Kapilavastu is the wrong pair. But Videha-Mithila and Moriya-Pippalivana appear in neither NCERT source. Marked untaught; the vajji_gana_sangha exam_note states exactly which pairs the books support and which they do not.

Which of the sixteen Mahajanapadas ultimately founded an empire (official key: Magadha). Fully taught: Magadha became the most powerful mahajanapada between the sixth and fourth centuries BCE (lehs102 p. 31) and its growth culminated in the Mauryan Empire (lehs102 p. 32).

Which Buddhist text gives an account of the 16 Mahajanapadas (official key: Anguttara Nikaya). NCERT (lehs102 p. 29) says only that early Buddhist and Jaina texts mention the sixteen states; it never names the Anguttara Nikaya. The Buddhist text NCERT does name is the Digha Nikaya, for the account of the Vajjis (fess105 p. 49). Source gap; the sixteen_mahajanapadas exam_note gives the exam answer and the NCERT position side by side.

When did Alexander invade India (official key: 326 B.C.). Primary HIS-04, alt HIS-06. Alexander's coming, his reaching the Beas and his soldiers' refusal are taught (fess105 p. 48), but neither NCERT chapter used gives the year 326 BCE — fess105 dates it only as 'more than 2300 years ago'. Source gap for the exact year; the towards_empire exam_note states the exam answer and flags the gap.
